talks.title: DIY AI: Build Your Own Digital InfoSec Team with BYOLLM
talks.teaser: Explains how self-hosted open-weight LLMs can support SOC triage, threat intel and document Q&A without sending data to third parties.
talks.summary:
Christian Taillon opens with the pressures security teams face: heavy workloads, junior analysts who must learn many tools quickly, and sensitive data that cannot always go to outside AI services. He presents large language models as a flexible, natural-language way to work with unstructured material such as logs, reports and threat feeds, and argues for running open-weight models on infrastructure the team controls.

The middle of the session covers the practical building blocks. He contrasts deterministic and probabilistic approaches, explains base versus instruction-tuned models, and shows how temperature and quantization affect output consistency, speed and memory use. He compares deployment options from frontier APIs to cloud-hosted and home-lab GPUs, then demonstrates a SOC analyst persona that combines standard operating procedures with an alert, and a retrieval-augmented setup that answers questions over local notes and PDFs. Tooling such as Ollama and Open WebUI appears along the way.

He closes with guardrails: low temperature for structured output, care with context windows, and isolating model runtimes in containers without root or outbound network access. A key warning concerns pickle-based model files, which can run code when loaded, so the safetensors format is recommended. Attendees leave with a sense of where local models fit into security operations and where they still fall short.

talks.title: Building Trust in AI: On Safe and Responsible Use of LLMs
talks.teaser: Surveys detection methods for AI-generated text and inference-time steering techniques that reduce harmful LLM outputs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the spread of generative AI and the accessibility of open-weight language models that can run on consumer GPUs. The speaker argues that this low barrier makes misuse easier and gives examples: LLM-written disinformation, AI-generated fake social media profiles, and multi-turn social-engineering conversations that convinced most test victims to share personal information. The talk also recognises legitimate uses such as code assistance and synthetic data generation.

The detection section groups methods into heuristic detectors based on log probabilities, watermarking that depends on model developers embedding a signal during generation, and fine-tuned classifiers, which performed best in the work presented. The main problem covered is generalising a detector to text from newer generators without labelled data, addressed by learning domain-invariant features across generators. For mitigation, the speaker explains why alignment and fine-tuning can erode safety behaviour and presents inference-time activation steering. Per-harm-category steering vectors are added to intermediate layers of Llama models, reducing unsafe responses, with some cost to helpfulness and a clear benefit when external safety guidance is used.

The final part describes an LLM-driven pipeline that produces counterfactual explanations for classifier decisions by extracting latent features and making minimal input edits that flip the label, with no extra training. A natural language inference example illustrated the approach. The practical takeaway is that detection must keep pace with new generators, and safety behaviour can be adjusted at inference time, though these methods remain research-stage.

talks.title: Whoops I Accidentally Hacked ASU
talks.teaser: Recounts how an accidental kiosk exploit at a university broadcast a Rick Astley video across campuses and what followed.
talks.summary:
Taaha Sayyed, a high school senior planning to study computer science at Arizona State University, describes how a frozen touchscreen directory kiosk at ASU's Mesa location led to an unplanned incident. After the kiosk crashed and exposed a Windows desktop, he used the on-screen keyboard to reach an elevated command prompt and launched a very long video of a Rick Astley song. He left without realizing the content was mirrored to signage at several campuses, including a large outdoor screen.

The middle of the talk covers the university's response: a summons from faculty, a review of camera footage, a note that a student in his position could face expulsion, a reflection process, and a written apology. Sayyed says the fix appeared to be disabling whatever input behavior he had triggered, and he questions whether that addresses deeper weaknesses. He also describes other things he noticed, including the scale of ASU's many locations, a site that appears thinly staffed, an exposed network switch, and room numbers visible in wireless traffic. He points out that there was no public bug bounty or clear reporting path for outside researchers.

His takeaways focus on kiosk hardening and disclosure. He argues for restricting kiosk accounts, closing off accessibility-based escapes, and giving finders a straightforward channel for reporting problems so that curiosity does not turn into a crisis.

talks.title: Digital Doppelgängers: The Dual Faces of Deepfake Technology
talks.teaser: Explains how deepfakes are built, the fraud cases they power, and the human checks that help catch them.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a hypothetical scenario in which a security analyst receives an urgent request, seemingly from a manager on a video call, to loosen network controls. From there the speaker explains how generative adversarial networks pit a generator against a discriminator, then sorts synthetic media into text, images, audio and video. Each category gets a concrete example: fabricated legal citations that a court rejected, a romance scam built on generated profile photos, and a robocall imitating a national leader.

The middle of the talk moves into live demonstrations, including a voice clone built from a short audio sample and a discussion of real-time face-swap tools running on webcams. Case studies cover a Hong Kong finance employee who wired about $25 million after a video call with what turned out to be fake colleagues, and a company that nearly hired a North Korean operative using a face-swapped identity, whose laptop was shipped to a laptop farm.

On detection, the speaker finds audio classifiers improving faster than video tools, which produced false positives and misses in testing. The practical defenses centre on people: asking unscripted questions, requesting a quick head turn, and confirming sensitive requests through a separate, known channel. Organisational steps include an AI-content proxy, clear policy, and frameworks such as the NIST AI RMF and MITRE ATLAS. The takeaway is to verify before acting and to keep a healthy level of skepticism.

talks.title: Digital damage control: misinformation, disinformation & negative effects during a crisis
talks.teaser: Shows how communications and security teams can track social media threats and respond to false narratives during a crisis.
talks.summary:
The session starts from the idea that social media often signals reputational risk before a security team sees any log entry. The presenters, a crisis communications practitioner and a chief information security officer with public-sector experience, argue that comms and security staff need a shared watch. They separate misinformation (false content shared without intent to deceive), disinformation (deliberately false content) and malinformation (true material used to cause harm), and explain that intent should shape how a response is scoped.

The middle of the talk walks through case studies. The Colonial Pipeline ransomware incident shows how a long silence let speculation and fuel hoarding fill the gap. The COVID-19 period brought scams, fake tracking apps and jargon-heavy warnings that increased confusion. Examples from the Russia-Ukraine conflict and recent US election cycles cover coordinated influence, a bot-driven surge in account registrations, a doctored image of supposed credentials, deepfake video, and social posts used to follow election staff in person.

For practitioners, the talk outlines a crisis team with a lead spokesperson and roles for PR, legal, compliance, HR and security. It suggests using out-of-band channels when internal email or systems may be compromised, and replacing vague phrasing with clear statements about what is being investigated and what is being done. Monitoring tools such as Hootsuite, Meltwater, Cision and Google Alerts are discussed, along with tabletop drills and documenting every incident for review.

talks.title: It is… Is Microsoft Active Directory Still Risky to Your Enterprise?
talks.teaser: Shows how common Active Directory misconfigurations enable domain takeover and how to audit and fix them with PowerShell.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a LinkedIn poll the speaker ran last year, where only 18 percent of respondents felt confident they could secure their Active Directory. He frames the directory as the most common target in intrusions. Attackers typically phish a user, escalate to local admin on a workstation, harvest credentials and work toward domain privileges. He argues that prevention matters more than detection and recovery, since attackers who gain domain control can easily plant persistence that survives restores.

The core of the talk is a set of AD configuration checks that can be verified with built-in tools and PowerShell. Privileged groups should be inventoried across default, application and service categories and audited recursively. A leftover primary group ID of 512 can quietly grant Domain Admin rights, and a demo showed that a standard user can query for such accounts. Other items include SID History leftovers, unexpected entries in AdminSDHolder that propagate to protected groups, unconstrained and constrained Kerberos delegation, service accounts with SPNs exposed to Kerberoasting, and Replicate Directory Changes rights on the domain root that enable DCSync.

The speaker stressed resetting the KRBTGT password twice in succession on a regular schedule, and recommended dumping ACLs with dsacls and monitoring privileged groups with a dedicated tool. He closed with a combined PowerShell audit bundle and noted that Azure AD has its own misconfiguration issues.

talks.title: The Pin Puller's Guide: A Hands-On Guide to Reverse Engineering iOS Applications
talks.teaser: Shows how to bypass iOS certificate pinning by reversing a training app in Ghidra and hooking it with Objection.
talks.summary:
The talk covers certificate pinning, the check that makes an app reject a proxy's substituted certificate and so blocks tools such as Burp. It explains why developers often dislike the control, since an expired pinned certificate can lock users out until an update ships. The demo target is the Damn Vulnerable iOS App on a jailbroken iPhone, where traffic routed through Burp fails the pin even after the Burp CA is trusted.

A quick Objection hook disables pinning and lets the request through, but the success message never appears, which shows the app skipped its intended code path. In Ghidra, the speaker searches for the error string, follows it to a branch driven by a boolean comparison, and sets aside simply patching that jump. Instead, they hook the NSData isEqual call, where the logged arguments show the app comparing against the server certificate rather than the Burp CA. A broad NSObject hook crashed the app, which is why a narrow hook point matters.

The fix replaces the bundled certificate with the server's leaf certificate, captured with OpenSSL and converted from PEM to DER. After the swap, the HTTPS request goes through and the original success message appears, so the intended code path runs. A source review confirms the app checks the certificate at index zero of the trust chain. For practitioners, a generic pinning disable can silently skip logic, and the same reversing workflow applies to other checks. The speaker argues pinning is usually defeated, so server-side controls deserve more effort.

talks.title: Top 10 Unexpected AI Systems Hacks that we did not see coming!
talks.teaser: Ranks ten surprising AI system attacks across organizations, consumers and critical infrastructure, paired with mitigations.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a rough map of the AI ecosystem, covering producers, deployers, users and bad actors, and notes that existing catalogues such as MITRE ATLAS and NIST AI RMF already list many known risks. The speakers then group their chosen attacks by who they hit: organizations, individuals and families, or infrastructure and markets. Each case is scored for likelihood, impact and how hard it is to prevent.

Organizational cases include a cloak meant to hide a person from thermal cameras guarding access points, spoken prompts that slip past audio guardrails, look-alike model names on public hubs that lead users to download tampered models, and poisoned feedback that lets fraud models miss real transactions. Consumer cases cover cloned celebrity images and voices used in romance and family emergency scams, smart glasses that profile strangers, and cloned voices that defeat single-factor bank verification. Macro cases include an automated trading flash crash and model extraction, linked to the market reaction after DeepSeek's release.

Suggested mitigations include guardrails tested across languages and phrasings, audits of model sources and data, circuit breakers for trading systems, multi-factor authentication rather than biometrics alone, tighter API key controls, family verification passwords, and AI inventories paired with data governance. The speakers note that no guardrail covers every edge case, so risks need prioritizing.

talks.title: Exploiting AI & Machine Learning Systems: Adversarial Attacks against Deep Learning Algorithms
talks.teaser: Walks through real-world attacks on AI systems, from road stickers fooling cars to poisoned training data and model extraction.
talks.summary:
Thomas Wilhelm opens with a short introduction and frames the talk as a high-level tour of how deep learning and language model systems can be pushed into bad decisions by hostile inputs. He argues that most AI attacks reuse familiar categories from web and network testing, applied to a different platform.

He then walks through public incidents. Small stickers on a road led a Tesla's driver-assist system to behave as if a lane change was needed, and a chatbot that absorbed hostile user input began producing offensive output. Masks defeated facial recognition used to unlock accounts, and a chatbot generated its own QR code and pressed a visitor for card details. He also covers tampered medical images that could produce false diagnoses. On the data side he discusses poisoning of crowdsourced datasets, where a single altered fact in a modified model spread quickly, and an encoded query that got a product search to list items tied to a dangerous chemical. Model inversion and extraction are illustrated with a leak from a DeepSeek deployment that exposed a database and API keys.

For defenders, he reviews layered controls: differential privacy, input sanitisation, adversarial training, federated learning with cross-checking across models, blockchain-based integrity records, anomaly detection and human review. His central point is that the integrity of training data matters most, and that a mix of these controls is needed. The talk closes with a checklist for red-team exercises and open questions from the audience.

talks.title: Machine Learning Models Gone Rogue - How to Reel Them Back In
talks.teaser: Shows how machine learning models can leak training data and which anonymization and privacy techniques reduce that risk.
talks.summary:
Monica Kay Royal opens by arguing that machine learning models are trained on sensitive personal data and can themselves become a privacy risk. She draws on the book Weapons of Math Destruction and a Cornell paper showing that models can memorize more of their training data than intended. She then walks through credit underwriting, targeted advertising and hiring, describing the personal signals each one draws on.

The middle of the talk covers defenses. She explains masking, generalization and pseudonymization as ways to remove identifiers, then describes how the Cornell researchers reconstructed training images from models using white-box and black-box attacks. Countermeasures include data minimization, adding noise through perturbation, and synthetic data. She also introduces k-anonymity, l-diversity and t-closeness for group privacy, noting the tradeoff with data utility.

The closing section turns to governance. Following the book's argument, she suggests revisiting success metrics that reward only profit and efficiency, adding feedback loops and transparency, and running algorithmic audits. She flags regulatory gaps, such as personality tests used in hiring, and calls for cross-disciplinary review involving law, ethics and audit. The talk ends with resources and a plug for her LinkedIn Learning course.
